<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-structured cases and executed the pressure-question protocol correctly, but B ultimately controlled the decisive clash. B's core "seller cannot be its own gatekeeper" narrative was reinforced across rounds by concrete historical patterns (Cyprus abolished, Malta and Portugal only tightened under external EU pressure, scandals recurring), and B's closing skillfully weaponized A's own concession that "Schengen exposure attaches to every residence permit" into a "zero marginal security benefit, plus unresolved corruption risk" argument that A never fully neutralized — A's best answer (screening intensity is the only remaining variable) was asserted but not decisively defended against B's counter that alternative channels are discretionary rather than lax. A's strongest unrebutted win was the housing sub-argument, and A's pressure questions forced a real concession from B ("I can't point to a single publicized security failure" in residency-only tracks), but A's own responses to B's parallel pressure questions leaned on deflection ("an agency that doesn't exist" answered with "PRO's Europe doesn't exist either") rather than a concrete existing fix. A also incurred a real execution cost, being clipped for length in two separate speeches versus B's one, losing concluding lines in exactly the rounds meant to crystallize comparison. On balance B provided the cleaner, more damaging final synthesis.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's turn to A's own admission that "Schengen exposure attaches to every residence permit" (A2.6/A4.7) into the closing claim that golden visas therefore add "zero marginal exposure over the alternatives" while still carrying unique self-policing/corruption risk (B5.1) was the most decisive exchange, since A never fully dislodged it beyond reasserting screening intensity without new support.</best_rebuttal>
